Q: EWS request - How to send an email with another email in attachment? A:

You can't do that in EWS (you can in MAPI) in EWS you need to either create an Item Attachment or use the Mime Content https://gsexdev.blogspot.com/2013/07/forwarding-message-as-attachment-using.html and attach that if its anything other then an email this isn't a great idea because you will loose fidelity. If this is Exchange Online note these methods are going to stop working soon due to EWS depreciations. In Microsoft Graph if you need to do this you look at doing everything client side the send the message as mime https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/outlook-send-mime-message

Q: What should I choose for a strong Full Stack foundation: Python and Django or JavaScript and Node.js as a backend? A:

The answer is: Yes.

Both Python with Django and Javascript with Node.js are popular options. Neither is more optimal than the other. They are designed for roughly the same work, and there are many examples of great projects in both.

And there are other popular, productive languages besides these. Java, C#, Go, Rust, Ruby, Elixir, and many others.

If you are a full stack web developer, you will not use just one language or framework. You will move from job to job, where they have chosen different languages. You will be expected to adapt to the technology they are using.

That's a good thing. Learning new programming languages is something software developers should be doing every year or two. Even if you prefer one language, studying and trying other languages can give you more insight into your favorite language.

Q: I am looking for best HL7 Integration tools A:

I've been working with HL7 message flows (inbound/outbound) in a healthcare system for a while now, and wanted to share my experience with HL7Soup for anyone evaluating HL7 tooling.

We actually had an in-house HL7 processing service that we built ourselves, handled parsing, OBX segments, base64 extraction, the usual stuff you deal with when you're moving HL7 messages through a custom pipeline. It worked, but once I started using HL7Soup alongside it for debugging and validation, it became pretty clear how much more polished a dedicated, specialized tool can be. We're actually in the process of shifting away from our in-house solution to HL7Soup now, and here's why:

  • It's built for exactly this — HL7Soup is a specialized tool for HL7 message handling, not a side feature bolted onto something else. That focus shows up everywhere, from how it parses messages to how it surfaces problems.

  • Integration flexibility — its handling of incoming and outgoing HL7 messages is genuinely great. It gives you a lot of options to modify and customize how messages are handled on both ends, which is really useful when your flows aren't perfectly standard (and let's be honest, whose HL7 flows ever are). The flexibility it provides here is really amazing compared to hardcoding that logic yourself.

  • No release cycle just to change a requirement — this is the big one for us. With our in-house service, any change to message handling meant a new release, and if you've got multiple clients, that means upgrading all of them. With HL7Soup, most of that same flexibility is just a settings change. The readiness is already built in, you're not waiting on a dev cycle to accommodate a new requirement.

  • Message inspection — being able to drill into a message segment-by-segment, with clear labeling of fields/components/subcomponents, is way faster than eyeballing raw pipe-delimited text or stepping through your own parser in a debugger.

  • Error identification — HL7Soup flags malformed segments and structural issues immediately, instead of finding out three steps downstream when a stored proc chokes on unexpected NULLs or a weird OBX value type.

  • Message comparison/testing — sending test messages and visually diffing what goes in vs what comes out saved a ton of time compared to writing one-off scripts to do the same thing.

In-house solutions aren't pointless, ours was tailored to our exact business logic, but maintaining that flexibility long-term, especially across multiple client deployments, became a real overhead. That's ultimately what tipped us toward moving to HL7Soup. It's the best HL7 tool I've used so far, hands down.

If your systems have HL7 flowing in and out and you're maintaining your own solution, it's worth seriously evaluating HL7Soup against the overhead of doing it yourself.

Q: How to make weak set or weak map iterable in ES6? A:

No the contents of a WeakMap are not accessible by design, and there is no iterability.

A key property of Weak Maps is the inability to enumerate their keys. This is necessary to prevent attackers observing the internal behavior of other systems in the environment which share weakly-mapped objects. Should the number or names of items in the collection be discoverable from the API, even if the values aren't, WeakMap instances might create a side channel where one was previously not available.
